newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian CCB earnings soar ahead of French alliance.
newsitem.headline: Belgian CCB earnings soar ahead of French alliance.

text.p: Belgian publicly-owned bank Credit Communal de Belgique/Gemeentekrediet van Belgie (CCB) published a solid rise in first-half earnings growth on Wednesday ahead of its planned alliance with French Credit Local de France (CLF).
CCB, Belgium's second-largest bank, said its first-half 1996 group net profit jumped 41.3 percent to 5.41 billion Belgian francs ($173.5 million) from 3.83 billion in the first half.

CCB chief executive officer Francois Narmon told a news conference that capital gains on CCB's investment portfolio and higher profits from financial services were the main reasons for the strong earnings.
He also pointed to a 300 million franc fall in provisions, mainly at CCB's 52-percent owned Luxembourg unit Banque Internationale a Luxembourg (BIL) and to good cost control.
Narmon warned that second-half profit would not be the same.
"We will have a good second half, but it seems ruled out that we would see a repeat of the 40 percent earnings growth."
He also said the strong 1996 half-year earnings growth was due to the fact that the year-earlier period had been weak.
Narmon denied CCB had made a special effort to book strong earnings growth ahead of the planned listing of its shares in November, an operation which is part of its planned alliance with CLF.

"People think we did this on purpose ahead of the bourse listing. That is not true, but it suits us well," he said. "Now that we are ready to merge with CLF it was especially important that our balance sheet adequately reflect reality."
Narmon also said that he expected CCB shareholders -- Belgium's municipal and regional public authorities -- would approve its planned alliance with CLF.
The partnership between CCB and CLF will create the 22nd largest bank in Europe and the largest European financial institution specialising in loans to local and regional public authorities.
The two banks are not merging. Their alliance involves setting up a complex holding structure, in which the two will take cross-holdings in each other's share capital. ($1=31.19 Belgian Franc)
